chunks: Muhammad ibn Abi Umair narrated from Mis'm Kirdin who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who broke the bone of a dead body. He said: 'Its sanctity as a dead body is greater than its sanctity while alive, so there is no contradiction between these narrations and the first narration, because nothing in them indicates that its sanctity as a dead body is like its sanctity while alive regarding the obligation of the complete blood-money upon the one who severs its head. It is permissible that what is meant by that is the liability for punishment regarding that, just as he deserves it if he did it to a living one.'
ai.seo_question: What is the difference in legal ruling between breaking the bone of a living person and a dead person in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In *Al-Istibsar*, Shaykh al-Tusi records Imam al-Sadiq’s (peace be upon him) nuanced resolution of an apparent contradiction regarding the sanctity (*hurmat*) of a deceased person versus the living. The Imam clarifies that while the spiritual sanctity of the dead is greater, the specific legal penalty of complete *diyah* (blood money) for bone-breaking is not obligatory as it is for the living; rather, the 'punishment' refers to the general liability (*istihqaq al-iqab*) incurred by the act itself, distinguishing between ritual sanctity and juridical compensation.
